lessons.title: From Talwandi to the Bein
lessons.dek: A village boy who asked uncomfortable questions grew into the First Guru. This is how Guru Nanak Dev Ji's mission began.
keyPoints: Guru Nanak Dev Ji was born in 1469 in Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan.
He worked as a storekeeper in Sultanpur Lodhi, where around 1499 he had a life-changing experience in the Bein river.
He taught three practices: remembering the Divine, earning an honest living, and sharing with others.

content.text: Guru Nanak Dev Ji was born in 1469 in Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, a village west of Lahore. Today it is called Nankana Sahib, and it lies in Pakistan. His father, Mehta Kalu, kept the village accounts. His mother was Mata Tripta. His older sister, Bebe Nanaki, is remembered as one of the first people to recognise that her brother was unusual.
Most of what we know about his childhood comes from the
janamsakhis
, collections of stories about his life written down after he died. They describe a thoughtful boy who argued with his teachers and was more interested in big questions than in the family business.
One of the best-known stories is the
Sacha Sauda

, the "true bargain". His father gave him money to trade at a market. On the way, he met a group of hungry holy men and spent all of it feeding them. When his father was angry, Nanak said he had made the most profitable deal possible.

As a young man he married Mata Sulakhni, and they had two sons, Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das. He moved to Sultanpur Lodhi, where Bebe Nanaki lived with her husband, and took a job as a storekeeper for the local governor, Daulat Khan Lodi. People remembered him as honest and generous with the grain in his care.
Each morning, before dawn, he bathed in the nearby Bein river and sat in meditation.

Around 1499, the janamsakhis say, he went into the Bein and did not come back. His friends searched the banks for three days and feared he had drowned. When he returned, he was changed. He sat silently for a time, and when he spoke, his first words were remembered like this:

blocks.english: There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.

content.text: He did not mean that religions did not exist. He meant that God does not see people by the labels they give themselves, and that what matters is how a person lives.
From this point he began to teach. His message is summed up in the words that open Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the Mool Mantar, which begins with
Ik Onkar
, "One Creator":

blocks.gurmukhi: ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ ॥
blocks.translit: Ik Onkār sat nām kartā purakh nirbhau nirvair akāl mūrat ajūnī saibhaṅ gur prasād
blocks.english: One Creator. Truth is the Name. Creative being, without fear, without hate, timeless in form, beyond birth, self-existent, known by the Guru's grace.
blocks.attribution: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 1 (one common translation)

content.text: He also taught a practical path built on three practices that Sikhs still describe today:
naam japna
, remembering the Divine;
kirat karni
, earning an honest living; and
vand chhakna
, sharing with others.

Almost everything we know about Guru Nanak Dev Ji's early life comes from the janamsakhis, which were written down decades after his death and differ from one another in their details and dates. Some historians, such as W.H. McLeod, read them mainly as devotional literature and are cautious about treating individual stories as history. Others, such as Harbans Singh, see them as preserving real memories of the Guru, shaped by the people who passed them on. Both views agree on the outline: the birth at Talwandi, the years at Sultanpur Lodhi, and a turning point that launched his mission.

quiz.prompt: Where was Guru Nanak Dev Ji born?

options.label: Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib

quiz.explanation: He was born in 1469 in Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now called Nankana Sahib, in present-day Pakistan.

quiz.prompt: What job did he hold in Sultanpur Lodhi?

options.label: Storekeeper for the governor, Daulat Khan Lodi

quiz.explanation: He looked after the governor's stores. Village accountant was his father's job in Talwandi.

quiz.prompt: In the Sacha Sauda story, what did he do with the money for trading?

options.label: Gave it back to his father
Fed a group of hungry holy men

quiz.explanation: He called feeding the hungry the "true bargain", the best trade he could make.

quiz.prompt: Which practice means earning an honest living?
quiz.explanation: Kirat karni is honest work. Naam japna is remembering the Divine, and vand chhakna is sharing.

lessons.title: The Udasis
lessons.dek: For about twenty years Guru Nanak Dev Ji travelled on foot, with a Muslim musician at his side, to talk with people of every faith.
keyPoints: For about twenty years Guru Nanak Dev Ji made long journeys, called udasis, with Bhai Mardana.
He taught through song and through simple actions that made people question empty ritual.
The story of Bhai Lalo puts honest work at the centre of religious life.
Details of the journeys come mainly from the janamsakhis, and historians debate them.

content.text: After his experience at the Bein, Guru Nanak Dev Ji did not stay in Sultanpur Lodhi. He set out on a series of long journeys known as the
udasis
. Tradition describes four main journeys, east, south, north and west, which took him across much of South Asia and beyond.
He did not travel alone. Bhai Mardana, a Muslim musician from Talwandi who had known him since childhood, went with him and played the
rabab
while the Guru sang. Their partnership was itself a message: a Hindu-born teacher and a Muslim musician, making music together about one Creator.
Guru Nanak Dev Ji taught through song. Many of the hymns he composed on these journeys were later collected in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, and they are still sung in every
gurdwara
today.
The janamsakhis remember him less for long sermons than for simple actions that made people think.

At Hardwar, on the Ganges, he saw pilgrims throwing water towards the rising sun as an offering to their ancestors. He began throwing water in the opposite direction. When people asked what he was doing, he said he was watering his fields in Punjab. If their water could reach the sun, his could surely reach a few hundred miles.

In the west, tradition says he travelled as far as Mecca. When he lay down to rest with his feet towards the Kaaba, a man angrily told him to move. He replied by asking the man to turn his feet in a direction where God was not.

At Saidpur, now Eminabad in Pakistan, he chose to stay with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter, instead of accepting a feast from Malik Bhago, a rich official. In the story, the Guru takes bread from each of them and squeezes it. Milk flows from Bhai Lalo's bread, earned by honest work, and blood from Malik Bhago's, earned by exploiting others.
The story puts
kirat karni
, honest living, at the centre of what it means to be religious.

While Guru Nanak Dev Ji was in Saidpur, the town was attacked by the army of Babur, who would go on to found the Mughal Empire. The Guru described the suffering he saw in a set of hymns known as the Babarvani, which are part of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. They are among the earliest eyewitness responses to Babur's invasion, and they speak openly against the cruelty of rulers.

The overall picture of long journeys is widely accepted, but the details are debated. The janamsakhis disagree about the order, length and destinations of the udasis, and some of the farthest journeys, such as those to Mecca, Baghdad and Sri Lanka, are known mainly from tradition. Historians such as W.H. McLeod have argued that we cannot confirm many specific places. Others point to long-standing local traditions and gurdwaras at sites associated with the Guru as evidence that his travels were remembered across a very wide area.

quiz.prompt: Who travelled with Guru Nanak Dev Ji on the udasis?
quiz.explanation: Bhai Mardana, a Muslim musician from Talwandi, played the rabab as the Guru sang.

quiz.prompt: At Hardwar, why did he throw water in the opposite direction?

options.label: To make people question whether the ritual could work

quiz.explanation: He said he was watering his fields in Punjab, gently asking whether water could really reach ancestors near the sun.

quiz.prompt: In the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago, what does the milk in Bhai Lalo's bread stand for?
quiz.explanation: Bhai Lalo's bread came from honest labour, kirat karni. Malik Bhago's came from exploiting others.

quiz.prompt: What are the Babarvani hymns about?

options.label: The suffering caused by Babur's invasion

quiz.explanation: Guru Nanak Dev Ji witnessed Babur's attack on Saidpur and described its cruelty in these hymns.

lessons.title: Kartarpur and the second Guru
lessons.dek: In his final years Guru Nanak Dev Ji farmed his own fields, built a community around shared meals and song, and chose a successor who was not his son.
keyPoints: Guru Nanak Dev Ji spent his final years at Kartarpur, farming his own fields among the community.
Langar and pangat made equality part of everyday life.
He chose Bhai Lehna, renamed Angad, as the second Guru instead of his own sons.
Kartarpur is in Pakistan. Since 2019 a corridor lets pilgrims from India visit.

content.text: When his travels ended, Guru Nanak Dev Ji settled at Kartarpur, a town he had founded on the banks of the Ravi river. He lived there with his family for the rest of his life, and it became the first Sikh community.
At Kartarpur the Guru did not live off offerings. He worked his own fields. The three practices he had taught on his journeys became the shape of an ordinary day.
Mornings and evenings began with hymns sung together by the
sangat
. Food was cooked and shared in the
langar
, where everyone sat together in a
pangat
, rich and poor, high caste and low, on the same floor. Visitors could see that equality was not just something the Guru preached. It was how the community ate dinner.

One of the people drawn to Kartarpur was Bhai Lehna, from the village of Khadur. He had been a devotee of the goddess Durga, but after hearing a hymn of Guru Nanak Dev Ji he came to meet him and stayed.
The janamsakhis tell many stories of his devotion and
seva
, doing whatever the Guru asked without hesitation, even when the Guru's own sons refused. Guru Nanak Dev Ji gave him a new name, Angad. It is often explained as coming from
ang
, a limb: someone who had become part of the Guru himself.

Before he died in 1539, Guru Nanak Dev Ji named Angad as the next Guru, passing over his own sons. This decision set a pattern that mattered for the future: the Guruship would pass to the person most fit for it, not automatically to the next in the family.

A well-known tradition says that after his death, his Hindu and Muslim followers disagreed over whether to cremate or bury him. When they lifted the sheet covering his body, they found only flowers, which they divided between them. At Kartarpur today there is both a memorial and a grave.

Guru Angad Dev Ji led the Sikhs from Khadur from 1539 to 1552. His wife, Mata Khivi, ran the langar and became known for her generosity. Guru Angad Dev Ji is credited with developing and popularising the
Gurmukhi
script, in which Punjabi and
Gurbani
are written.

Kartarpur lies in Pakistan, only a few kilometres from the border with India. For decades Sikh pilgrims from India could only look at the gurdwara through binoculars from the Indian side. In November 2019 the Kartarpur Corridor opened, allowing pilgrims to cross and visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib without a visa.

Historians agree that Guru Nanak Dev Ji spent his last years at Kartarpur and appointed Guru Angad Dev Ji as his successor in 1539. Dates for when he settled there vary between sources. On the Gurmukhi script, scholars generally agree that forms of it existed before Guru Angad Dev Ji, and they discuss his role as refining and spreading it rather than inventing it from nothing.

quiz.prompt: On which river was Kartarpur founded?
quiz.explanation: Guru Nanak Dev Ji founded Kartarpur on the banks of the Ravi.

options.label: A hymn sung in the morning
Sitting together in rows to eat, as equals

quiz.explanation: In pangat, everyone sits on the same floor to eat langar, with no distinction of caste or status.

quiz.prompt: Who did Guru Nanak Dev Ji choose as the second Guru?
quiz.explanation: He passed over his sons and chose Bhai Lehna, whom he renamed Angad.

glossary.english: One Creator. The opening of the Mool Mantar and of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.
Spiritual teacher and guide. Sikhs recognise ten human Gurus and Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the eternal Guru.
The Guru's word: the compositions of the Gurus and others collected in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.
The script in which Punjabi and Gurbani are written.
Traditional accounts of Guru Nanak Dev Ji's life, written down after his lifetime.
Remembering and meditating on the Divine Name.
Earning an honest living through your own work.
Sharing what you have with others.
One of Guru Nanak Dev Ji's long journeys to teach and meet people of many faiths.
A plucked string instrument. Bhai Mardana played it as Guru Nanak Dev Ji sang.
The congregation; people gathered together in the Guru's presence.
The free community kitchen, where everyone eats together as equals.
Sitting together in rows to eat langar, with no distinction of caste or status.
"The Guru's door": a Sikh place of worship.

places.name: Nankana Sahib
places.summary: Birthplace of Guru Nanak Dev Ji in 1469. Gurdwara Janam Asthan stands on the site.

places.name: Sultanpur Lodhi
places.summary: Where Guru Nanak Dev Ji worked as a storekeeper and, around 1499, had his experience in the Bein river.

places.name: Eminabad
places.summary: Home of Bhai Lalo. Guru Nanak Dev Ji witnessed Babur's attack on the town and described it in the Babarvani hymns.

places.name: Kartarpur
places.today: Punjab, Pakistan, close to the border
places.summary: The town Guru Nanak Dev Ji founded on the Ravi, where he lived his final years and died in 1539.

places.name: Khadur Sahib
places.summary: Home of Bhai Lehna, who became Guru Angad Dev Ji and led the Sikhs from here from 1539 to 1552.

places.name: Goindwal Sahib
places.summary: On the Beas river. The centre of the Sikh community under Guru Amar Das Ji.

places.name: Amritsar
places.summary: Founded by Guru Ram Das Ji. Guru Arjan Dev Ji installed the Adi Granth at Harmandir Sahib here in 1604.

places.name: Lahore
places.summary: Provincial capital under the Mughals. Guru Arjan Dev Ji was martyred here in 1606.

places.name: Kiratpur Sahib
places.summary: In the Shivalik foothills. Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji spent his later years here.

places.name: Anandpur Sahib
places.summary: Where Guru Gobind Singh Ji founded the Khalsa on Vaisakhi in 1699.
